articles.title: How the biggest renewable energy project in US history finally got built
articles.content:
This story was originally published by Vox and is reproduced here as part of the Climate Desk collaboration.​

When the sun goes down, the wind picks up in central New Mexico, whipping through arid canyons with a ghostly howl that for centuries, locals have likened to the wails of the folkloric ghost La Llorona.

A few hours east of Albuquerque, this June, those gusts began powering the largest wind farm this continent has ever seen, twirling over 900 colossal steel turbines. Each is as tall as the Statue of Liberty, scattered across a patch of desert roughly the size of Chicago. They plug into a 550-mile transmission line stitched across the Southwest and are now powering over 1 million homes — as far away as California.

The SunZia Wind and Transmission project is a rare 21st-century triumph of American infrastructure, an engineering marvel that generates more electricity than the Hoover Dam. When the turbines came online this spring, they immediately broke records for wind-generated power in California’s energy supply, where solar power may rule the day, but the winds of New Mexico increasingly fuel the night.

After years of stagnant power growth, the U.S. is absolutely starving for more electricity, with demand projected to rise by 25 percent by the end of this decade, and a staggering 78 percent by 2050. Enormous as this challenge might seem, it may ultimately be the catalyst the country needs to dramatically dial up its renewable energy infrastructure, so that the years to come are powered not by gas or coal, but by clean energy sources like the sun and the wind. By next summer, the project will have prevented about 9 million metric tons of carbon dioxide from entering the atmosphere, according to Pattern Energy, the project’s developer.

To support our nonprofit environmental journalism, please consider disabling your ad-blocker to allow ads on Grist. Here's How

For decades, however, it seemed the project would remain little more than a spectral dream.

“It works!” This was the call Hunter Armistead, Pattern’s CEO, remembers getting from his head engineer when the turbines came online for the very first time. “We were creating power, and it was showing up 550 miles away in Phoenix, almost as if it was magic.” During the ribbon-cutting for the wind farm, some construction workers showed off massive new turbine tattoos. “It’s their pride that for the rest of their lives, they can drive by and tell their kid, ‘I did this,’” Armistead said.

But SunZia almost didn’t get built at all. It is not just the project’s scale that makes it remarkable, but the utter morass its developers slogged through to bring it online. The project spanned five presidential administrations, an ownership change, a major reroute, and a standoff with a U.S. military base.

It also involved a series of lawsuits from local tribal communities and environmental advocates, some of which remain pending even as the turbines now finally whirl. Building any renewable megaproject requires vast amounts of space, and hyper-specific natural conditions, like a wind that blows at night or a reliably sun-soaked desert plain. Then getting that energy to major cities means traversing some of the most pristine, spectacular natural corridors this nation has left, and particularly in the Southwest, rubbing up against the sacred lands of local tribal communities.

To support our nonprofit environmental journalism, please consider disabling your ad-blocker to allow ads on Grist. Here's How

The decades-long saga to settle some of these tensions has turned SunZia into a helpful lesson, and for many, deserved or not, it became the ultimate poster child for permitting reform. And for many years, the country’s need for power didn’t seem to call for such a wildly ambitious project anyway. But in the interim, as the world changed, SunZia changed too, becoming — at least in some places — a better and more collaborative project than it was when it began. And now, with a nation finally focused on building more clean energy megaprojects, it can offer a glimpse of what’s to come, even a blueprint of what could be.

The real reason(s) it took so long for SunZia to get built

When SunZia was first proposed in 2006, the same year Twitter went online, coal was still the most important electricity source in America, and the nation’s appetite for electricity had remained nearly flat year after year.

And for the next 17 years, SunZia flailed, never even breaking ground. It ping-ponged between financial and regulatory purgatories that most commentators have attributed to endless permitting delays. There were, for example, a few state-level permitting debacles, with New Mexico rejecting SunZia’s initial transmission route in 2018. Even after such interstate power lines get federal approval, they often need to wait years longer for approvals from every state in which their project passes.

Senator Martin Heinrich of New Mexico, for one, has cited SunZia as a key impetus for his co-sponsoring the Senate’s new plan for permitting reform. This would make it easier for the federal government to coordinate approval processes for interstate transmission lines, ensuring that they happen concurrently and preventing one state from dragging its heels.

The project had faced one particularly large and sticky permitting challenge: getting the power through the White Sands Missile Range. But this, and other challenges, were eventually resolved relatively quickly. And to David Hayes, who served as deputy secretary of the Department of the Interior during the Obama administration, this suggests that financing hamstrung the project even more than red tape.

“The facts are the facts, and they got their permit,” said Hayes — all the way back in 2015, not long after the Obama administration put SunZia on a “fast track” to approval. “So we finally got the permit done. Hooray, right? And then nothing happens. Nothing happens.”

Part of that was the fact that the two states where SunZia wanted to build its transmission lines were not entirely on board. But it was also the sheer expense involved in building the project, especially given that the federal approval required burying parts of the transmission line near the missile range. Moreover, even if everything went perfectly with the project’s permitting process, it might have been impossible to build SunZia back then, said Armistead, because “we really didn’t have the market need for it.”

The U.S. simply wasn’t as ravenous for new electricity as it is right now, and the importance of building out the future of energy was not enticing enough for investors on its own.

But, refusing to die a slow death of a thousand permitting blockades or financial setbacks, SunZia instead evolved. Pattern Energy, initially only in charge of developing the wind farm portion of the project, took over the transmission line project in 2022. Around that time, SunZia applied for a revised federal permit, one that would circumvent the missile range, and within less than two years — a relative sprint for federal bureaucracy — they had a new approval in hand. Then came $11 billion in financing from several global financial institutions, pension funds, and clean energy investors. Then, a few years of construction time later, the Americas’ biggest wind farm was finally switched on.

And more massive projects like this will be needed, because nowadays “there is no longer the excuse” of a market unready for high volumes of clean energy, Armistead told me. “It is game time, and we’re supposed to get this done.”

What America’s biggest clean energy project got right

One of the secrets to SunZia’s ultimate success in New Mexico was the project’s ability to strike compromises, even with some of its earliest critics. In some cases, a bunch of birds.

Right about now, the earliest migratory birds, like the crimson-capped sandhill crane, have begun arriving at their Southwestern wintering grounds, not far from some of SunZia’s newly operational high-voltage transmission lines.

This crane had nearly gone extinct before, driven in part by an explosion of new hydroelectric dams in the early 20th century, whose construction dried out local wetlands. SunZia’s initial route, which was planned across one of the most congested flyways in the country, threatened them again, birders feared, alongside other migratory species who might accidentally fly into the new power lines, a threat believed to kill millions of birds nationwide each year.

While SunZia’s original developer, the Southwestern Power Group, was largely unmoved by those concerns, said Sarah Rose, vice president of climate at the National Audubon Society, the nonprofit found an unusually receptive partner to compromise when Pattern Energy took over.

“They took their role as a project developer really seriously,” she said, “and I think they engaged with us with a lot of integrity and a lot of good faith.” Under a rerouting plan, original power lines were moved north, erected next to existing infrastructure, or affixed with visual warning systems or bird diverters. Not only did the changes make the bird advocates happy, but they were enough to help convince the New Mexico Public Regulation Commission, which had rejected SunZia’s permit application a few years earlier in part due to these concerns, to unanimously approve the project in 2022.

To be clear, not everybody believed Pattern always made the appropriate compromises, especially in Arizona, where SunZia’s route remained unchanged under the new management. Peter Else, a local environmentalist, has spent years fighting SunZia in court over its intrusion into the scenic San Pedro Valley, a region that is sacred to Indigenous communities such as the Tohono O’odham Nation and San Carlos Apache Tribe. To see it marred by more power lines through the landscape has been like “mourning a death,” Else said, “like an ecological homicide.”

He would have liked to see SunZia try to run the valley’s new power lines alongside existing ones, as it managed to do in parts of New Mexico, a process that Armistead told me would not have been possible because the Arizona portion of the line “was already put to bed,” and the original federal permit had found the valley to be “the least impactful and best route.” A lawsuit from the Tohono O’odham Nation and San Carlos Apache Tribe accusing SunZia and the Department of the Interior of failing to protect the valley remains pending.

Of course, climate change threatens many of these regions more than a single power line. In the two decades it took SunZia to begin pumping clean energy across state lines, waves of extreme heat have taken tens of thousands of American lives, and the entire Southwest has continued in a mega drought unseen in the past 1,200 years.

These are some of the very concerns that SunZia seeks, in part, to combat. And if we want to avoid even more heat deaths, extreme droughts, more flash floods, and more habitat destruction, then we probably will need a lot more facilities like it, some of which will require hard tradeoffs.

But they aren’t doomed always to. It may have taken SunZia over a decade to learn that lesson, but for future megaprojects, the blueprint may already be there. The nearby 280-mile high-voltage Southline Transmission Project spanning parts of Arizona and New Mexico is set to begin construction next year, and it’s been so intentional about minimizing its ecological and cultural impact that even Else praised it as a good idea. And this approach could pave the way for even more essential large-scale projects like it. “If more folks could come to the table looking for solutions as opposed to expecting conflict,” Rose said, “I think we would be able to move a lot more quickly.” Ideally, it won’t take another 20 years.

articles.personality_title: Largest U.S. wind farm begins powering over 1 million homes
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – For many years, the U.S. struggled to expand its renewable energy infrastructure despite growing electricity needs. Large projects like wind farms require special locations with strong winds or sun and must cross protected lands, leading to long delays in approval and construction.

**What happened** – In June 2024, the SunZia Wind and Transmission project in New Mexico officially started producing electricity. It is the biggest wind farm in North America, with over 900 turbines as tall as the Statue of Liberty spread across a desert area the size of Chicago. The energy travels through a 550-mile transmission line to supply power to more than 1 million homes, reaching as far as California.

**Impact** – This project generates more electricity than the Hoover Dam and helps reduce carbon dioxide emissions by about 9 million metric tons each year. It shows how large renewable energy projects can succeed despite years of legal, environmental, and financial challenges. The project also worked with environmental groups to protect birds and respected some concerns of local Indigenous communities, setting a new example for future clean energy efforts.

**What's next step** – The success of SunZia encourages more large-scale renewable projects to be built faster. For example, the Southline Transmission Project in Arizona and New Mexico is planned to start construction soon with careful attention to ecological and cultural impacts. New laws are also being proposed to speed up approvals for projects that cross state lines.

**One-sentence takeaway** – After nearly two decades of challenges, the SunZia wind farm now powers over a million homes with clean energy, offering a model for faster, more thoughtful renewable projects in the U.S.
articles.personality_title_fr: La plus grande ferme éolienne des États-Unis alimente plus d’un million de foyers
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Depuis plusieurs années, les États-Unis ont eu du mal à développer leurs infrastructures d’énergie renouvelable malgré une demande croissante en électricité. Les grands projets comme les parcs éoliens nécessitent des endroits particuliers avec beaucoup de vent ou de soleil et doivent traverser des terres protégées, ce qui cause de longs retards dans les autorisations et la construction.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – En juin 2024, le projet éolien et de transmission SunZia au Nouveau-Mexique a officiellement commencé à produire de l’électricité. C’est la plus grande ferme éolienne en Amérique du Nord, avec plus de 900 turbines aussi hautes que la Statue de la Liberté, réparties sur un désert de la taille de Chicago. L’énergie est transmise par une ligne de 550 miles qui alimente plus d’un million de foyers, jusqu’en Californie.

**Impact** – Ce projet génère plus d’électricité que le barrage Hoover et aide à réduire les émissions de dioxyde de carbone d’environ 9 millions de tonnes chaque année. Il montre que les grands projets d’énergie renouvelable peuvent réussir malgré des années de défis juridiques, environnementaux et financiers. Le projet a aussi collaboré avec des groupes environnementaux pour protéger les oiseaux et a pris en compte certaines préoccupations des communautés autochtones locales, établissant un nouvel exemple pour l’avenir.

**Prochaine étape** – Le succès de SunZia encourage la construction plus rapide d’autres grands projets renouvelables. Par exemple, le projet de transmission Southline en Arizona et au Nouveau-Mexique devrait bientôt commencer avec une attention particulière aux impacts écologiques et culturels. De nouvelles lois sont aussi proposées pour accélérer les autorisations des projets traversant plusieurs États.

**Message en une phrase** – Après près de vingt ans de défis, la ferme éolienne SunZia alimente désormais plus d’un million de foyers en énergie propre, offrant un modèle pour des projets renouvelables plus rapides et réfléchis aux États-Unis.
articles.personality_title_es: La mayor granja eólica de EE.UU. ya suministra energía a más de un millón de hogares
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Durante muchos años, Estados Unidos tuvo dificultades para ampliar su infraestructura de energía renovable a pesar de la creciente demanda de electricidad. Los grandes proyectos como parques eólicos requieren lugares especiales con mucho viento o sol y deben atravesar tierras protegidas, lo que provoca largos retrasos en las aprobaciones y la construcción.

**Qué pasó** – En junio de 2024, el proyecto eólico y de transmisión SunZia en Nuevo México comenzó oficialmente a producir electricidad. Es la granja eólica más grande de América del Norte, con más de 900 turbinas tan altas como la Estatua de la Libertad, repartidas en un desierto del tamaño de Chicago. La energía viaja por una línea de transmisión de 550 millas para alimentar a más de un millón de hogares, llegando hasta California.

**Impacto** – Este proyecto genera más electricidad que la presa Hoover y ayuda a reducir las emisiones de dióxido de carbono en aproximadamente 9 millones de toneladas cada año. Muestra cómo los grandes proyectos de energía renovable pueden tener éxito a pesar de años de desafíos legales, ambientales y financieros. El proyecto también trabajó con grupos ambientalistas para proteger a las aves y respetó algunas preocupaciones de las comunidades indígenas locales, estableciendo un nuevo ejemplo para futuros esfuerzos de energía limpia.

**Próximo paso** – El éxito de SunZia fomenta la construcción más rápida de otros grandes proyectos renovables. Por ejemplo, el Proyecto de Transmisión Southline en Arizona y Nuevo México está planeado para comenzar pronto con atención cuidadosa a los impactos ecológicos y culturales. También se están proponiendo nuevas leyes para acelerar las aprobaciones de proyectos que cruzan líneas estatales.

**Mensaje en una frase** – Después de casi dos décadas de desafíos, la granja eólica SunZia ahora alimenta con energía limpia a más de un millón de hogares, ofreciendo un modelo para proyectos renovables más rápidos y conscientes en EE.UU.

articles.title: COP17: Nations chart ‘Yerevan Pathway’ to speed up action for nature
articles.summary: At the halfway mark to 2030, countries meeting in Armenia have agreed a roadmap to accelerate action for nature, after a global review found the world off track to meet its biodiversity targets.
articles.content:
Agreement was formalised through the Yerevan Pathway as the UN Biodiversity Conference (COP17) closed in the Armenian capital on Saturday.

It sets out priorities for the four years left to deliver the 23 targets of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework.

Mixed message

“We cannot protect nature while continuing to finance its destruction,” said Astrid Schomaker, Executive Secretary of the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD).

The pathway calls on countries to tackle subsidies that harm nature and to increase financial, scientific and technical support for developing countries.

It also calls for national budgets and economic decisions to be aligned with the framework, and for stronger monitoring and reporting.

“Over these two weeks we have demonstrated that differences can be bridged, commitments can become decisions and cooperation can deliver,” said COP17 President Hambardzum Matevosyan.

Progress made

Parties adopted nearly 50 decisions, covering areas including protected areas and forests, wildlife management, invasive alien species, marine and coastal biodiversity, and synthetic biology.

After intensive negotiations, they also agreed the Sevan Guidelines.

These set the rules of operation for a new permanent body strengthening the role of Indigenous Peoples and local communities in shaping global biodiversity policy.

Funding boost

Nearly $2 billion in new biodiversity funding was announced. This included $560 million under the Global Environment Facility’s latest replenishment and $500 million through the Species Recovery Alliance.

Another $330 million is going to the Value Nature Fund, which aims to mobilise private capital for nature.

Other initiatives included a new biodiversity bond and investment incubator launched by the Asian Development Bank, and new indicators to improve biodiversity monitoring and accountability.

Spirit of compromise

“In Yerevan, we saw environmental multilateralism prevail once again,” said Inger Andersen, Executive Director of the UN Environment Programme (UNEP).

“Countries came together, found the spirit of compromise and allowed us to agree important decisions that will support real progress for people and for planet.”

The next conference, COP18, will be held in Ecuador, with two years remaining to achieve the targets.

“Ultimately, the test is not what governments agreed in Yerevan, but what they change when they return home,” said Ms. Schomaker.
articles.source: UN News - Global perspective Human stories
articles.reasoning: The article reports a significant global agreement at COP17 to accelerate biodiversity action through the Yerevan Pathway, including concrete financial commitments, policy priorities, and enhanced roles for Indigenous Peoples. This represents a meaningful and broad impact on global biodiversity conservation efforts with detailed context and tangible outcomes.
articles.personality_title: Global leaders agree on Yerevan Pathway to speed up nature protection
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – In 2022, countries met in Yerevan, Armenia, for the 17th UN Biodiversity Conference (COP17). This meeting happens every two years to help protect nature around the world. The world is halfway to 2030, the target year to meet key goals for saving plants, animals, and ecosystems, but progress was found to be too slow.

**What happened** – At the end of COP17, countries agreed on a new plan called the Yerevan Pathway. This plan sets clear priorities for the next four years to reach 23 important biodiversity targets. Leaders promised to stop funding activities that harm nature and to support poorer countries with money, science, and technology. They also made new rules to include Indigenous Peoples and local communities in decision-making about nature.

**Impact** – This agreement is important because it brings together nearly 50 decisions on protecting forests, wildlife, oceans, and more. Nearly $2 billion was promised to help save species and habitats, showing a strong financial commitment. The inclusion of Indigenous Peoples is unique because it recognizes their vital role in caring for nature. The Yerevan Pathway creates a clearer path forward after earlier warnings that the world was not on track to meet biodiversity goals.

**What's next step** – The next big meeting, COP18, will take place in Ecuador in two years. Countries will report on their progress and hopefully speed up efforts to protect nature. The real test will be how governments change their actions back home, using the agreements made in Yerevan.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Countries at COP17 agreed on the Yerevan Pathway with clear actions and funding to protect nature faster and involve Indigenous Peoples more closely in global decisions.
articles.personality_title_fr: Les dirigeants mondiaux adoptent la voie de Yerevan pour accélérer la protection de la nature
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – En 2022, des pays se sont réunis à Erevan, en Arménie, pour la 17e Conférence des Nations Unies sur la biodiversité (COP17). Cette réunion a lieu tous les deux ans pour aider à protéger la nature dans le monde. Nous sommes à mi-chemin de 2030, l'année cible pour atteindre des objectifs clés pour sauver les plantes, les animaux et les écosystèmes, mais les progrès étaient jugés trop lents.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – À la fin de la COP17, les pays ont adopté un nouveau plan appelé la voie de Yerevan. Ce plan fixe des priorités claires pour les quatre prochaines années afin d’atteindre 23 objectifs importants pour la biodiversité. Les dirigeants ont promis d’arrêter de financer des activités qui nuisent à la nature et de soutenir les pays pauvres avec de l’argent, de la science et de la technologie. Ils ont aussi établi de nouvelles règles pour inclure les peuples autochtones et les communautés locales dans la prise de décision sur la nature.

**Impact** – Cet accord est important parce qu’il regroupe près de 50 décisions sur la protection des forêts, de la faune, des océans, et plus encore. Près de 2 milliards de dollars ont été promis pour aider à sauver les espèces et les habitats, montrant un engagement financier fort. L’inclusion des peuples autochtones est unique car elle reconnaît leur rôle vital dans la protection de la nature. La voie de Yerevan crée un chemin plus clair après les avertissements précédents que le monde n’était pas sur la bonne voie pour atteindre les objectifs de biodiversité.

**Prochaine étape** – La prochaine grande réunion, la COP18, aura lieu en Équateur dans deux ans. Les pays feront le point sur leurs progrès et accéléreront, espérons-le, les efforts pour protéger la nature. Le vrai test sera de voir comment les gouvernements changent leurs actions chez eux, en utilisant les accords pris à Erevan.

**En une phrase** – À la COP17, les pays ont adopté la voie de Yerevan avec des actions claires et des financements pour protéger la nature plus rapidement et impliquer davantage les peuples autochtones dans les décisions mondiales.
articles.personality_title_es: Líderes mundiales acuerdan la Ruta de Ereván para acelerar la protección de la naturaleza
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – En 2022, países se reunieron en Ereván, Armenia, para la 17ª Conferencia de las Naciones Unidas sobre Biodiversidad (COP17). Esta reunión ocurre cada dos años para ayudar a proteger la naturaleza en todo el mundo. Estamos a mitad del camino hacia 2030, el año objetivo para cumplir metas clave para salvar plantas, animales y ecosistemas, pero se encontró que el progreso es demasiado lento.

**Qué pasó** – Al final de la COP17, los países acordaron un nuevo plan llamado la Ruta de Ereván. Este plan establece prioridades claras para los próximos cuatro años para cumplir 23 objetivos importantes de biodiversidad. Los líderes prometieron dejar de financiar actividades que dañan la naturaleza y apoyar a los países pobres con dinero, ciencia y tecnología. También crearon nuevas reglas para incluir a los pueblos indígenas y comunidades locales en la toma de decisiones sobre la naturaleza.

**Impacto** – Este acuerdo es importante porque reúne casi 50 decisiones sobre la protección de bosques, vida silvestre, océanos y más. Se prometieron casi 2 mil millones de dólares para ayudar a salvar especies y hábitats, mostrando un fuerte compromiso financiero. La inclusión de los pueblos indígenas es única porque reconoce su papel vital en el cuidado de la naturaleza. La Ruta de Ereván crea un camino más claro después de advertencias anteriores de que el mundo no estaba en camino de cumplir las metas de biodiversidad.

**Próximo paso** – La próxima gran reunión, la COP18, se realizará en Ecuador dentro de dos años. Los países informarán sobre su progreso y, con suerte, acelerarán los esfuerzos para proteger la naturaleza. La verdadera prueba será cómo cambian sus acciones los gobiernos en casa usando los acuerdos hechos en Ereván.

**Una frase clave** – En la COP17, los países acordaron la Ruta de Ereván con acciones claras y financiamiento para proteger la naturaleza más rápido e involucrar más a los pueblos indígenas en decisiones globales.

articles.title: The Great Barrier Reef's most notorious coral killer may actually be helping it
articles.summary: Crown-of-thorns starfish are notorious for devouring coral reefs, but surprising new research reveals these spiny predators may actually help reefs thrive when their populations are kept in check. Scientists studying Australia's Great Barrier Reef discovered that nearly 75% of observed starfish feeding events left behind living coral tissue, rather than destroying entire colonies. By feeding on fast-growing, dominant corals, the starfish create opportunities for slower-growing species to survive, potentially increasing coral biodiversity.
articles.content:
Crown-of-thorns starfish (COTS) are among the most feared creatures on coral reefs. Covered in sharp, toxin-filled spines, these predators are notorious for consuming coral and leaving widespread destruction in their wake.

However, new research from the University of Sydney suggests these infamous reef destroyers may also have a surprisingly beneficial side. When their populations remain under control, crown-of-thorns starfish can help maintain healthy coral communities and support greater biodiversity.

Native to Australia's Great Barrier Reef, these coral-eating starfish have caused enormous damage during population explosions. Since the 1960s, the reef has experienced four major outbreaks, occurring roughly every 15 years. Declining numbers of natural predators, including tritons and several species of reef fish, have made the Great Barrier Reef and other marine ecosystems more vulnerable to these destructive events.

Scientists Discover That Coral Often Survives Starfish Attacks

In a study published in Ecology and Evolution, researchers investigated what happens to coral after crown-of-thorns starfish feed on it. The team examined feeding scars and remaining living tissue at the University of Sydney's One Tree Island Research Station, located on the Great Barrier Reef.

The study sites were within protected areas where healthy fish populations help keep starfish numbers under control. Unlike other parts of the reef that experience devastating outbreaks, these locations maintain relatively low populations of crown-of-thorns starfish.

The results revealed an unexpected pattern. A team led by Dr. Shawna Foo found that living coral tissue survived nearly 75 percent of the observed feeding events.

"At One Tree Reef, COTS appear to consume a relatively consistent amount of coral during each meal and move on, rather than demolishing the entire coral colony," said Dr. Foo, a University of Sydney Horizon Fellow in the School of Life and Environmental Sciences. "This meant live coral tissue remnants were frequently left behind."

How Coral-Eating Starfish Can Boost Reef Biodiversity

The discovery suggests that small populations of crown-of-thorns starfish may play an important role in maintaining the balance of coral reef ecosystems.

Some coral species grow quickly and can take over large areas, limiting the space available to slower-growing varieties. By feeding on these dominant species, crown-of-thorns starfish may create opportunities for other corals to survive and establish themselves.

The researchers found that surviving fragments of fast-growing Acroporidae corals did not regenerate over the areas damaged by starfish feeding. In contrast, regrowth occurred primarily among slower-growing Montipora and Porites corals.

"By feeding on fast-growing corals such as Acropora, low-density COTS populations create space for slower-growing coral species to persist, helping to increase coral diversity," Dr. Foo said.

This finding challenges the idea that all coral consumption by crown-of-thorns starfish is harmful. Under the right conditions, their feeding behavior may actually prevent a few dominant coral species from taking over the reef.

Why Eliminating Crown-of-Thorns Starfish Could Be a Mistake

Despite these potential benefits, researchers caution that large outbreaks of crown-of-thorns starfish remain a serious threat. When their numbers increase dramatically, they can destroy extensive areas of coral, leaving reefs struggling to recover.

The key difference is whether starfish populations remain at naturally manageable levels or grow into destructive outbreaks.

"It's important to distinguish between COTS populations performing their natural role as coral predators and outbreaks causing sustained reef decline."

Although the research was conducted mainly in protected areas with healthy fish populations and little risk of major outbreaks, the findings could help scientists and conservation managers improve strategies for controlling crown-of-thorns starfish.

In particular, the results suggest that removing every starfish may not be the best approach once an outbreak has been brought under control.

"The implications of our work can help us decide when and why culling should occur and the ecological endpoint of a cull. Once an outbreak is suppressed, the goal should not necessarily be to eliminate COTS entirely. Culling needs to be complemented by strong marine management to protect COTS predators and keep COTS populations in check."

Research co-author Professor Maria Byrne connected the findings to a well-established ecological concept.

"The results are consistent with the intermediate disturbance hypothesis, an important framework in ecology and conservation."

According to this hypothesis, ecosystems can benefit from occasional, moderate disturbances that prevent any single species from becoming too dominant.

The research suggests that crown-of-thorns starfish may be an example of this natural balancing process. While uncontrolled outbreaks can devastate coral reefs, smaller populations may help maintain the diversity that makes these ecosystems so valuable.

articles.title: California legalizes balcony solar for renters and beyond
articles.summary:
BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM California just gave apartment renters a shot at solar. Governor Gavin Newsom signed a bill legalizing plug-in solar panels, also called balcony solar, clearing the way for a technology that doesn’t require a roof you own, a contractor, or tens of thousands of dollars up front. Compliant models are […]
The post California legalizes balcony solar for renters and beyond first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News.
articles.content:
BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM

California just gave apartment renters a shot at solar. Governor Gavin Newsom signed a bill legalizing plug-in solar panels, also called balcony solar, clearing the way for a technology that doesn’t require a roof you own, a contractor, or tens of thousands of dollars up front. Compliant models are expected to hit shelves in mid-2027.

How the hardware works

The hardware is minimal: a few small panels, an inverter, and cables. The panels can hang from a balcony railing, mount outside a window, or sit in a backyard. Existing models run from $300 to $2,200, much cheaper than a rooftop installation because you set them up yourself. In Germany, where they’re already common, you just plug them into a wall outlet. California’s version has more certification requirements for now, but that’s where the law is pointed.

Who is historically left out of rooftop solar?

Rooftop solar has always had prerequisites. You need to own your home, have a qualifying roof, and either have capital or qualify for financing. That locked out renters from day one, along with a lot of low-income households and anyone in a multifamily building.

“These small, easy-to-use solar panels will give everyone, including renters, the relief they desperately need on our outrageous energy bills,” said state Senator Scott Wiener, who wrote the bill. It passed with bipartisan support.

The benefits of plug-in

A plug-in system can cover up to 20 percent of a home’s electricity needs and save as much as $500 a year for a small apartment. California electric bills have climbed hard over the past few years, so that number means something to a lot of people.

The registration overhaul

The registration change matters nearly as much as the legalization. Under the old rules, adding a plug-in panel meant completing the same interconnection paperwork required for a full rooftop system, which could cost up to $800 and take days. Advocates noted that process cost more than the panels themselves in some cases. Under the new law, registration is free and immediate.

Systems must stay under 1,200 watts per home, pass third-party safety certification, and include protection against backfeeding electricity into the grid during outages. Products currently on the market don’t meet those standards yet, so the old registration process still applies for now. The sale of non-compliant systems becomes illegal in 2030, and the law runs from 2027 to January 1, 2030.

“The market is sending a clear signal to manufacturers that they need to develop a California system,” said Cora Stryker, co-founder of Bright Saver, a plug-in solar advocacy group.

California is the tenth state to pass this kind of law. Utah went first in March 2025; Colorado, Virginia, and Maine followed. But California is the country’s largest electricity market, which means manufacturers pay attention in a different way. What advocates have been describing for years, plug-in solar on the shelf at a hardware store, is now a reasonable near-term prospect.
